solution:
Given: \( C = 15.0\ \mu\mathrm{F} = 15 \times 10^{-6} \) F, \( e_{\mathrm{rms}} = 220 \) V, \( f = 50 \) Hz.
Capacitive reactance:
\( X_C = \frac{1}{2\pi f C} = \frac{1}{2 \times 3.142 \times 50 \times 15 \times 10^{-6}} = \frac{1}{4.713 \times 10^{-3}} \)
\( \therefore X_C = 212.2\ \Omega \)
rms current:
\( i_{\mathrm{rms}} = \frac{e_{\mathrm{rms}}}{X_C} = \frac{220}{212.2} = 1.037 \) A
Peak current:
\( i_0 = \sqrt{2}\, i_{\mathrm{rms}} = 1.414 \times 1.037 \)
\( \therefore i_0 = 1.466 \) A
If the frequency is doubled: \( X_C = \frac{1}{2\pi f C} \) is inversely proportional to f, so the capacitive reactance is HALVED, to \( 106.1\ \Omega \). The applied voltage is unchanged, so the current \( i_{\mathrm{rms}} = \frac{e_{\mathrm{rms}}}{X_C} \) is DOUBLED, to \( 2.074 \) A.

Given: \( R = 10\ \Omega \) in series with a capacitor, power factor \( \cos\phi = 0.5 \), \( f = 100 \) Hz. (The 80 V supply is not needed to find C.)
The power factor of a series RC circuit is \( \cos\phi = \frac{R}{Z} \), so
\( Z = \frac{R}{\cos\phi} = \frac{10}{0.5} = 20\ \Omega \)
Since \( Z = \sqrt{R^2 + X_C^2} \),
\( X_C = \sqrt{Z^2 - R^2} = \sqrt{(20)^2 - (10)^2} = \sqrt{400 - 100} = \sqrt{300} \)
\( \therefore X_C = 17.32\ \Omega \)
Now \( X_C = \frac{1}{2\pi f C} \), so
\( C = \frac{1}{2\pi f X_C} = \frac{1}{2 \times 3.142 \times 100 \times 17.32} = \frac{1}{10884} \)
\( \therefore C = 9.188 \times 10^{-5} \) F \( = 91.88\ \mu\mathrm{F} \)

Given: \( e = 220 \sin 100\pi t \), so \( e_0 = 220 \) V and \( \omega = 100\pi \) rad/s; \( L = \frac{1}{\pi} \) H. The circuit contains inductance only.
Inductive reactance:
\( X_L = \omega L = 100\pi \times \frac{1}{\pi} = 100\ \Omega \)
Peak current:
\( i_0 = \frac{e_0}{X_L} = \frac{220}{100} = 2.2 \) A
In a purely inductive circuit the current LAGS the emf by \( \frac{\pi}{2} \), so the instantaneous current is
\( i = i_0 \sin \left( \omega t - \frac{\pi}{2} \right) \)
\( \therefore i = 2.2 \sin \left( 100\pi t - \frac{\pi}{2} \right) \) A
An AC galvanometer (a hot-wire type meter) reads the rms value, not the peak value:
\( i_{\mathrm{rms}} = \frac{i_0}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{2.2}{1.414} \)
\( \therefore i_{\mathrm{rms}} = 1.556 \) A

**(B)** 0.7071

The power factor of an a.c. circuit is \(\cos\phi\), where \(\phi\) is the phase difference between the voltage and the current.

Here \(\phi = 45^{\circ}\), so

\(\cos 45^{\circ} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\)

\(\therefore\) the power factor is \(0.7071\).

A value of 1.0 would mean a purely resistive circuit with voltage and current in phase, which is not the case here.
note: 1/1.414 = 0.7072, not the 0.7071 the next line states; the intermediate dropped.

solution:
Given: \( C = 100\ \mu\mathrm{F} = 100 \times 10^{-6} \) F, \( R = 50\ \Omega \), \( L = 0.5 \) H, \( e_{\mathrm{rms}} = 110 \) V, \( f = 50 \) Hz.
Reactances:
\( X_L = 2\pi f L = 2 \times 3.142 \times 50 \times 0.5 = 157.1\ \Omega \)
\( X_C = \frac{1}{2\pi f C} = \frac{1}{2 \times 3.142 \times 50 \times 100 \times 10^{-6}} = \frac{1}{3.142 \times 10^{-2}} = 31.83\ \Omega \)
Net reactance (inductance dominated, since \( X_L > X_C \)):
\( X_L - X_C = 157.1 - 31.83 = 125.3\ \Omega \)
Impedance:
\( Z = \sqrt{R^2 + \left( X_L - X_C \right)^2} = \sqrt{(50)^2 + (125.3)^2} = \sqrt{2500 + 15700} = \sqrt{18200} \)
\( \therefore Z = 134.9\ \Omega \)
rms current:
\( i_{\mathrm{rms}} = \frac{e_{\mathrm{rms}}}{Z} = \frac{110}{134.9} \)
\( \therefore i_{\mathrm{rms}} = 0.8154 \) A

Given \( e = 8 \sin (628.4\, t) \). Comparing this with the standard form \( e = e_0 \sin \omega t \):

(i) Peak value of the e.m.f.

\( \therefore e_0 = 8 \) V

(ii) \( \omega = 628.4 \) rad/s, and \( \omega = 2\pi f \)

\( \therefore f = \frac{\omega}{2\pi} = \frac{628.4}{2 \times 3.142} = \frac{628.4}{6.284} \)

\( \therefore f = 100 \) Hz

(iii) The period of the e.m.f. is

\( T = \frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{100} = 0.01 \) s \( = 10 \) ms

so the instant \( t = 10 \) ms is exactly the end of one complete cycle. The instantaneous value there is

\( e = e_0 \sin \omega t = 8 \sin \left( 628.4 \times 10 \times 10^{-3} \right) = 8 \sin (6.284) \)

where the angle is in radian. Since \( 6.284 \) rad \( = 2\pi \) rad and \( \sin 2\pi = 0 \),

\( \therefore e \approx 0 \) V

Check: the e.m.f. starts from \( e = 8 \sin 0 = 0 \) at \( t = 0 \), and after one whole period the waveform has returned to the value it started from, so a zero at \( t = T \) is consistent.
note: 6.284 rad is 2 pi only to the 3.142 used, so 8 sin(6.284) is about 0 (0.0065 V), not exactly 0.

solution:
Given
\( e = 140 \sin 3142\, t \)
\( R = 50\ \Omega \)
i) On comparing with \( e = e_0 \sin \omega t \)
We get \( \omega = 3142 \), \( e_0 = 140 \) V
\( \omega = 2\pi f \quad \therefore f = \frac{\omega}{2\pi} = \frac{3142}{2 \times 3.142} = 500 \) Hz
(ii) \( e_0 = 140 \) V
\( e_{\mathrm{rms}} = \frac{e_0}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{140}{\sqrt{2}} = 98.99 \) V
\( \therefore i_{\mathrm{rms}} = \frac{e_{\mathrm{rms}}}{R} = \frac{98.99}{50} = 1.98 \) A
note: Divides 99.29 where the line before gives e_rms = 98.99 V.

solution:
Given

\( e = 140 \sin (314.2\, t) \)

\( R = 50\ \Omega \)

(i) On comparing with \( e = e_0 \sin \omega t \) we get \( e_0 = 140 \) V and \( \omega = 314.2 \) rad/s.

\( \omega = 2\pi f \)

\( \therefore f = \frac{\omega}{2\pi} = \frac{314.2}{2 \times 3.142} = \frac{314.2}{6.284} \)

\( \therefore f = 50 \) Hz

(ii) \( e_{\mathrm{rms}} = \frac{e_0}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{140}{1.414} = 99.01 \) V

The resistor is pure, so the current through it is in phase with the voltage across it and Ohm's law applies directly to the rms values:

\( \therefore i_{\mathrm{rms}} = \frac{e_{\mathrm{rms}}}{R} = \frac{99.01}{50} = 1.98 \) A

Check: the peak current is \( i_0 = \frac{e_0}{R} = \frac{140}{50} = 2.8 \) A, and \( \frac{i_0}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{2.8}{1.414} = 1.98 \) A, the same value by the other route.
note: 140/1.414 = 99.01 V (98.99 is 140/sqrt 2 unrounded); i_rms = 1.98 A unchanged.

solution:
Given: \( C = 25\ \mu\mathrm{F} = 25 \times 10^{-6} \) F, \( L = 0.10 \) H, \( R = 25\ \Omega \), \( e = 310 \sin 314\, t \), so \( e_0 = 310 \) V and \( \omega = 314 \) rad/s.
Frequency:
\( f = \frac{\omega}{2\pi} = \frac{314}{2 \times 3.142} = 50 \) Hz
Reactances:
\( X_L = \omega L = 314 \times 0.10 = 31.4\ \Omega \)
\( X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C} = \frac{1}{314 \times 25 \times 10^{-6}} = \frac{1}{7.85 \times 10^{-3}} = 127.4\ \Omega \)
Net reactance (the circuit is capacitance dominated, since \( X_C > X_L \)):
\( X = X_C - X_L = 127.39 - 31.4 = 95.99\ \Omega \)
Impedance:
\( Z = \sqrt{R^2 + X^2} = \sqrt{(25)^2 + (95.99)^2} = \sqrt{625 + 9214} = \sqrt{9839} \)
\( \therefore Z = 99.19\ \Omega \)
Current:
\( e_{\mathrm{rms}} = \frac{e_0}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{310}{1.414} = 219.2 \) V
\( i_{\mathrm{rms}} = \frac{e_{\mathrm{rms}}}{Z} = \frac{219.2}{99.19} \)
\( \therefore i_{\mathrm{rms}} = 2.210 \) A
Phase angle:
\( \tan\phi = \frac{X}{R} = \frac{95.99}{25} = 3.840 \)
\( \therefore \phi = \tan^{-1}(3.840) = 75.4^\circ = 1.316 \) rad
Since \( X_C > X_L \), the current LEADS the applied emf by 1.316 rad.

**Decay constant of \(^{14}\text{C}\).** \(T_{1/2} = 5730\ \text{years} = 5730 \times 3.154 \times 10^{7} = 1.807 \times 10^{11}\ \text{s}\)

\(\lambda = \dfrac{\ln 2}{T_{1/2}} = \dfrac{0.693}{1.807 \times 10^{11}} = 3.835 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{s}^{-1}\)

**(a) Fraction of carbon atoms that were \(^{14}\text{C}\).** For one gram of carbon the activity is 0.255 Bq, so from \(A = \lambda N\),

\(N(^{14}\text{C}) = \dfrac{0.255}{3.835 \times 10^{-12}} = 6.65 \times 10^{10}\) atoms per gram

The total number of carbon atoms in one gram is \(\dfrac{6.022 \times 10^{23}}{12} = 5.018 \times 10^{22}\).

\(\text{fraction} = \dfrac{6.65 \times 10^{10}}{5.018 \times 10^{22}} = 1.33 \times 10^{-12}\)

That is, **about four \(^{14}\text{C}\) atoms in every \(3 \times 10^{12}\) carbon atoms.**

**(b) Age of the specimen.** The specimen gives 174 decays in one hour from 500 mg, so per gram

\(A = \dfrac{174}{3600 \times 0.5} = 0.0967\ \text{Bq g}^{-1}\)

When it died its activity per gram was the atmospheric value \(A_0 = 0.255\ \text{Bq g}^{-1}\). From \(A = A_0 e^{-\lambda t}\),

\(\lambda t = \ln\dfrac{0.255}{0.0967} = \ln(2.637) = 0.9697\)

\(t = \dfrac{0.9697}{3.835 \times 10^{-12}} = 2.529 \times 10^{11}\ \text{s}\)

\(t = \dfrac{2.529 \times 10^{11}}{3.154 \times 10^{7}}\)

**The specimen is about 8020 years old.**

The radius of a nucleus X with mass number \(A\) is given by \(R_X = R_0 A^{\frac{1}{3}}\), where \(R_0 = 1.2 \times 10^{-15}\ \text{m}\)

Thus, the radius of \(^{70}\text{Ge}\) is

\(R_{Ge} = 1.2 \times 10^{-15} \times 70^{1/3} = 4.946 \times 10^{-15}\ \text{m}\).

The density is given by \(\rho = \dfrac{3m_{Ge}}{4\pi R_{Ge}^{3}}\).

\(\therefore \rho = 3 \times 69.924 \times 1.66 \times \dfrac{10^{-27}}{4\pi\left(4.95 \times 10^{-15}\right)^{3}}\)

\(= 2.285 \times 10^{17}\ \text{kg m}^{-3}\).
note: 1.2e-15 x 70^(1/3) = 4.9455e-15 (printed 4.945); the density with the line's own 4.95e-15 is 2.285e17 (printed 2.292).

solution:
**Required activity.** \(1\ \text{Ci} = 3.7 \times 10^{10}\) decays per second, so

\(A = 10.0\ \text{mCi} = 10.0 \times 10^{-3} \times 3.7 \times 10^{10} = 3.7 \times 10^{8}\ \text{s}^{-1}\)

**Decay constant.** \(T_{1/2} = 5.3\ \text{years} = 5.3 \times 3.154 \times 10^{7} = 1.6716 \times 10^{8}\ \text{s}\)

\(\lambda = \dfrac{0.693}{1.6716 \times 10^{8}} = 4.146 \times 10^{-9}\ \text{s}^{-1}\)

**Number of nuclei needed.** From \(A = \lambda N\),

\(N = \dfrac{A}{\lambda} = \dfrac{3.7 \times 10^{8}}{4.146 \times 10^{-9}} = 8.924 \times 10^{16}\) nuclei

**Mass.** The gram atomic mass of \(^{60}_{27}\text{Co}\) is 60 g, so

\(m = \dfrac{N}{6.022 \times 10^{23}} \times 60 = \dfrac{8.924 \times 10^{16}}{6.022 \times 10^{23}} \times 60\)

**\(m = 8.89 \times 10^{-6}\) g**, i.e. about 8.9 micrograms of \(^{60}_{27}\text{Co}\).
note: 5.3 x 3.154e7 = 1.6716e8 s (printed 1.671e8); the later 4.146e-9 follows from 1.6716.

solution:
The disintegration rate is the activity \(A = \lambda N\).

**Decay constant.** \(T_{1/2} = 28\ \text{years} = 28 \times 3.154 \times 10^{7} = 8.831 \times 10^{8}\ \text{s}\)

\(\lambda = \dfrac{0.693}{T_{1/2}} = \dfrac{0.693}{8.831 \times 10^{8}} = 7.847 \times 10^{-10}\ \text{s}^{-1}\)

**Number of nuclei.** \(^{90}_{38}\text{Sr}\) has a gram atomic mass of 90 g, so 5 mg contains

\(N = \dfrac{5 \times 10^{-3}}{90} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 3.346 \times 10^{19}\) nuclei

**Activity.**

\(A = \lambda N = 7.847 \times 10^{-10} \times 3.346 \times 10^{19}\)

**\(A = 2.626 \times 10^{10}\) disintegrations per second** \((\text{i.e. } 2.626 \times 10^{10}\ \text{Bq}\), about 0.71 Ci).

The number of revolutions is the frequency of revolution multiplied by the time, \(N = f \times t\), where \(f = \dfrac{\mathrm{v}_n}{2\pi r_n}\).

For hydrogen \((Z = 1)\) in the second orbit \((n = 2)\):

\(\mathrm{v}_2 = \dfrac{e^{2}}{2\varepsilon_0 h n} = \dfrac{(1.602 \times 10^{-19})^{2}}{2 \times 8.854 \times 10^{-12} \times 6.626 \times 10^{-34} \times 2} = 1.094 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}\)

\(r_2 = \dfrac{n^{2}h^{2}\varepsilon_0}{\pi m_e e^{2}} = 4 \times 5.293 \times 10^{-11} = 2.117 \times 10^{-10}\ \text{m}\)

\(\therefore f = \dfrac{1.094 \times 10^{6}}{2\pi \times 2.117 \times 10^{-10}} = 8.225 \times 10^{14}\ \text{revolutions per second}\)

\(\therefore N = 8.225 \times 10^{14} \times 10^{-8}\)

**\(N = 8.225 \times 10^{6}\) revolutions**

**(a) Decay constant and mean lifetime.**

\(T_{1/2} = 272\ \text{d} = 272 \times 24 \times 3600 = 2.350 \times 10^{7}\ \text{s}\)

\(\lambda = \dfrac{0.693}{T_{1/2}} = \dfrac{0.693}{2.350 \times 10^{7}} = 2.95 \times 10^{-8}\ \text{s}^{-1}\)

\(\tau = \dfrac{1}{\lambda} = 3.39 \times 10^{7}\ \text{s}\) (about 392 days)

**(b) Number of nuclei in the source.**

\(A = 2.0\ \mu\text{Ci} = 2.0 \times 10^{-6} \times 3.7 \times 10^{10} = 7.4 \times 10^{4}\ \text{s}^{-1}\)

\(N = \dfrac{A}{\lambda} = \dfrac{7.4 \times 10^{4}}{2.95 \times 10^{-8}} = 2.51 \times 10^{12}\) nuclei

**(c) Activity after one year.**

\(t = 365\ \text{d}\), so \(\lambda t = 0.693 \times \dfrac{365}{272} = 0.9299\)

\(A(t) = A_0 e^{-\lambda t} = 2.0 \times e^{-0.9299} = 2.0 \times 0.3946\)

\(A(t) = 0.789\ \mu\text{Ci}\)

**Mean lifetime \(3.39 \times 10^{7}\) s, decay constant \(2.95 \times 10^{-8}\ \text{s}^{-1}\), \(2.51 \times 10^{12}\) nuclei, and the activity falls to \(0.789\ \mu\text{Ci}\) after one year.**
